figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Overall pre-training and fine-tuning procedures for BERT. Apart from output layers, the same architectures are used in both pre-training and fine-tuning. The same pre-trained model parameters are used to initialize models for different down-stream tasks. During fine-tuning, all parameters are fine-tuned. [CLS] is a special symbol added in front of every input example, and [SEP] is a special separator token (e.g. separating questions/answers).
figures.headline: Figure 1 shows BERT pre-training on unlabeled text and fine-tuning all parameters, with the same initial parameters for each downstream task.
citing_sentences: The question-answering example in Figure 1 will serve as a running example for this section.

Second, we add a learned embedding to every token indicating whether it belongs to sentence A or sentence B. As shown in Figure 1, we denote input embedding as $E$, the final hidden vector of the special [CLS] token as $C\in\mathbb{R}^{H}$, and the final hidden vector for the $i^{\rm th}$ input token as $T_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{H}$.
This step is presented in the left part of Figure 1.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: BERT input representation. The input embeddings are the sum of the token embeddings, the segmentation embeddings and the position embeddings.
figures.headline: Figure 2 shows that each BERT input embedding is the sum of token, segment and position embeddings.
citing_sentences: A visualization of this construction can be seen in Figure 2.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Differences in pre-training model architectures. BERT uses a bidirectional Transformer. OpenAI GPT uses a left-to-right Transformer. ELMo uses the concatenation of independently trained left-to-right and right-to-left LSTMs to generate features for downstream tasks. Among the three, only BERT representations are jointly conditioned on both left and right context in all layers. In addition to the architecture differences, BERT and OpenAI GPT are fine-tuning approaches, while ELMo is a feature-based approach.
figures.headline: Figure 3 shows that only BERT conditions on both left and right context in all layers, unlike OpenAI GPT and ELMo.

abstract:
We introduce a new language representation model called BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Unlike recent language representation models Peters et al. (2018a); Radford et al. (2018), BERT is designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers. As a result, the pre-trained BERT model can be fine-tuned with just one additional output layer to create state-of-the-art models for a wide range of tasks, such as question answering and language inference, without substantial task-specific architecture modifications.

BERT is conceptually simple and empirically powerful. It obtains new state-of-the-art results on eleven natural language processing tasks, including pushing the GLUE score to 80.5% (7.7% point absolute improvement), MultiNLI accuracy to 86.7% (4.6% absolute improvement), SQuAD v1.1 question answering Test F1 to 93.2 (1.5 point absolute improvement) and SQuAD v2.0 Test F1 to 83.1 (5.1 point absolute improvement).

sections.body: The section motivates BERT by arguing that unidirectional pre-training limits fine-tuning approaches, especially for token-level tasks such as question answering. BERT uses a masked language model objective, which randomly masks input tokens and predicts them from both left and right context, plus a next sentence prediction task. The section reports that BERT advances results on eleven NLP tasks. It also states that the code and pre-trained models are released on GitHub.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: BERT pre-trains deep bidirectional representations with masked language modeling and next sentence prediction, then fine-tunes them with one added output layer.

sections.body: This section reviews earlier pre-training approaches, including word embeddings, sentence embeddings, and ELMo, which concatenates independently trained left-to-right and right-to-left models. It also reviews OpenAI GPT, which is fine-tuned but uses unidirectional language modeling. Earlier work on transfer from supervised data, such as natural language inference and machine translation, is summarized as well. The section is a literature review and reports no new experimental results of its own.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Prior work used feature-based or unidirectional fine-tuning methods, while BERT is the first fine-tuning model that is deeply bidirectional.

sections.body: BERT has two steps: pre-training on unlabeled data, then fine-tuning all parameters on labeled downstream data. The paper reports two sizes, BERTBASE with L=12, H=768, A=12 and 110M total parameters, and BERTLARGE with L=24, H=1024, A=16 and 340M total parameters. Inputs use WordPiece embeddings with a 30,000 token vocabulary, and 15% of tokens are selected for masked prediction. The pre-training corpora are BooksCorpus (800M words) and English Wikipedia (2,500M words). Table 1 reports GLUE test results, where BERTLARGE averages 82.1 against 75.1 for OpenAI GPT.
sections.heading: BERT
sections.headline: BERT uses a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer, with masked language model and next sentence prediction pre-training on BooksCorpus and Wikipedia.

sections.body: BERT is fine-tuned on eleven tasks by adding one output layer, with learning rates chosen on the Dev set. On GLUE, BERTLARGE obtains a score of 80.5 on the official leaderboard, compared with 72.8 for OpenAI GPT, and MNLI accuracy improves by 4.6% absolute. On SQuAD v1.1, the ensemble with TriviaQA fine-tuning reaches 93.2 test F1, and on SQuAD v2.0 the single BERTLARGE model reaches 83.1 test F1. On SWAG, BERTLARGE reaches 86.3 test accuracy against 78.0 for OpenAI GPT. The section gives no limitation beyond noting that some large-model fine-tuning on small datasets was unstable.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: BERT reaches 80.5 on the GLUE leaderboard, 83.1 test F1 on SQuAD v2.0, and 93.2 test F1 on SQuAD v1.1 with TriviaQA data.

sections.body: The pre-training ablation in Table 5 compares BERTBASE with a model without next sentence prediction and a left-to-right model, on MNLI-m, QNLI, MRPC, SST-2 and SQuAD. The left-to-right model scores 77.8 F1 on SQuAD against 88.5 for BERTBASE. Table 6 shows that increasing layers and hidden size gives higher accuracy on MNLI-m, MRPC and SST-2, from 77.9 to 86.6 on MNLI-m. For NER, Table 7 shows that the feature-based approach with concatenated top four layers reaches 96.1 Dev F1, which is 0.3 F1 behind fine-tuning the full model. Results in Table 7 are averaged over 5 random restarts.
sections.heading: Ablation Studies
sections.headline: Ablations show next sentence prediction and bidirectional pre-training each improve results, and larger models improve small tasks.

sections.body: The conclusion states that transfer learning with language models makes unsupervised pre-training an integral part of many language understanding systems. It states that the paper's main contribution is extending these findings to deep bidirectional architectures, so that one pre-trained model can handle a broad set of NLP tasks. The section makes no new quantitative claims and does not restate specific results.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The paper concludes that bidirectional pre-training generalizes to a broad set of NLP tasks with one pre-trained model.

sections.body: Appendix A illustrates the masking procedure, which replaces selected tokens with [MASK] 80% of the time, a random word 10% of the time, and keeps the word 10% of the time. It gives the pre-training setup: batch size 256 sequences, 1,000,000 steps, Adam with learning rate 1e-4, and a 0.1 dropout probability. Appendix B describes the GLUE datasets. Appendix C reports ablations over training steps in Figure 5 and over masking strategies in Table 8, where fine-tuning is described as surprisingly insensitive to the masking choice.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists pre-training and fine-tuning hyperparameters, GLUE task descriptions, and additional ablations on training steps and masking strategies.
